title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Pursued by a French army of a hundred thousand men under Bonaparte's command, met by a hostile local population, losing faith in its allies, short of supplies, and forced to operate under conditions of war that no one had anticipated, the Russian army of thirty-five thousand under Kutuzov was retreating rapidly along the Danube. It halted when overtaken by the enemy and fought rearguard actions only as far as necessary to continue its retreat without losing its heavy equipment. There had been engagements at Lambach, Amstetten, and Melk, but despite the courage and endurance with which the Russians fought—acknowledged even by the enemy—the only result of these battles was an even faster retreat. The Austrian troops that had escaped capture at Ulm and joined Kutuzov at Braunau now broke away from the Russian army, leaving Kutuzov with nothing but his own weak and exhausted forces. The defense of Vienna was no longer thinkable. Instead of the offensive campaign whose plan, carefully devised according to the modern science of strategy, had been handed to Kutuzov in Vienna by the Austrian War Council, his sole remaining objective—and a nearly unattainable one—was to link up with the reinforcements marching from Russia without losing his army the way Mack had lost his at Ulm.

On October 28, Kutuzov crossed with his army to the left bank of the Danube and took up a position for the first time with the river between himself and the bulk of the French forces. On the thirtieth, he attacked Mortier's division on the left bank and shattered it. In this engagement, trophies were captured for the first time: banners, cannons, and two enemy generals. For the first time after two weeks of retreat, Russian troops had halted and, after a fight, had not only held the field but driven the French back. Though the troops were poorly clothed, exhausted, and had lost a third of their strength to dead, wounded, sick, and stragglers—though many of the sick and wounded had been left behind on the far side of the Danube with a letter entrusting them to the enemy's mercy—and though the large hospitals and houses in Krems that had been converted into military hospitals could no longer hold all the casualties—the stand at Krems and the victory over Mortier lifted the army's spirits considerably. Throughout the entire army and at headquarters, the most optimistic (though inaccurate) rumors were circulating: that Russian reinforcement columns were approaching, that the Austrians had won some victory, and that a frightened Bonaparte was in retreat.

Prince Andrei had served during the battle as aide to the Austrian General Schmidt, who was killed in the action. His horse had been shot from under him and a bullet had grazed his arm. As a mark of the commander in chief's special favor, he was chosen to carry the news of this victory to the Austrian court, which was now at Brünn rather than Vienna, since Vienna was threatened by the French. Despite his seemingly delicate build, Prince Andrei could endure physical hardship far better than many much stronger men. On the night of the battle, having arrived at Krems excited but not tired, with dispatches from Dokhturov for Kutuzov, he was immediately sent on with a special dispatch to Brünn. Being chosen for such a mission meant not only a reward but an important step toward promotion.

The night was dark but starry. The road showed black against the snow that had fallen the day before—the day of the battle. Replaying his impressions of the recent fight, pleasantly imagining the reaction his news of victory would produce, remembering the send-off from the commander in chief and his fellow officers, Prince Andrei raced along in a post chaise, savoring the feelings of a man who has finally begun to achieve a long-desired happiness. As soon as he closed his eyes, his ears filled with the rattle of wheels and the sensation of victory. Then he would start imagining that the Russians were fleeing and that he himself had been killed—but he quickly shook off the vision with a surge of joy, as if discovering all over again that none of it was true, that on the contrary, it was the French who had fled. He recalled every detail of the victory once more, and his own steady courage during the battle, and feeling reassured, he drifted off to sleep... The dark, starry night gave way to a bright, cheerful morning. The snow was melting in the sunshine, the horses galloped briskly, and on both sides of the road stretched forests of different kinds, fields, and villages.

At one of the relay stations he overtook a convoy of Russian wounded. The Russian officer in charge of the transport was sprawled in the front cart, shouting at a soldier with crude abuse. In each of the long German carts, six or more pale, dirty, bandaged men were being jolted over the rough road. Some were talking—he caught Russian words—and others were chewing bread. The more severely wounded watched in silence, with the dull curiosity of sick children, as the courier rushed past them.

Prince Andrei told his driver to stop and asked a soldier which battle they had been wounded in. "Day before yesterday, on the Danube," the soldier answered. Prince Andrei took out his purse and gave the man three gold coins.
"That's for all of them," he said to the officer who came up.
"Get well soon, lads!" he called to the soldiers. "There's still plenty to do."
"Any news, sir?" asked the officer, clearly eager to strike up a conversation.
"Good news! Drive on!" he shouted to his driver, and they galloped away.

It was already quite dark by the time Prince Andrei rattled over the cobblestone streets of Brünn and found himself surrounded by tall buildings, the glow of shop windows and house lamps, elegant carriages, and all the bustle of a large, lively city—always so appealing to a soldier after life in camp. Despite his rapid journey and sleepless night, he felt even more energized and alert as he pulled up to the palace than he had the day before. Only his eyes had a feverish gleam, and his thoughts followed one another with extraordinary speed and clarity. He relived the details of the battle once more—no longer hazy, but sharp and precise, framed in the concise form in which he imagined reporting them to Emperor Francis. He vividly anticipated the offhand questions that might be asked and the answers he would give. He expected to be ushered into the Emperor's presence immediately. At the main entrance to the palace, however, an official hurried out to meet him and, learning that he was a special messenger, directed him to a different entrance.
"To the right down the corridor, Your Excellency! There you'll find the adjutant on duty," the official said. "He will take you to the Minister of War."

The adjutant on duty met Prince Andrei, asked him to wait, and went in to see the minister. Five minutes later he returned and, bowing with exaggerated courtesy, led Prince Andrei along a corridor to the room where the Minister of War was working. The adjutant's elaborate politeness seemed designed to discourage any attempt at familiarity from the Russian messenger.

Prince Andrei's elated mood dimmed considerably as he approached the minister's door. He felt slighted, and without being fully aware of it, his sense of offense immediately hardened into a disdain that was entirely uncalled for. His quick mind instantly supplied a perspective that gave him the right to look down on both the adjutant and the minister. "Far from the smell of gunpowder, they probably think winning victories is easy!" he thought. His eyes narrowed scornfully as he entered the Minister of War's room with deliberately measured steps. This feeling of contempt only deepened when he saw the minister seated at a large table, reading documents and marking them with pencil notes, paying no attention whatsoever to his arrival for the first two or three minutes. A wax candle stood on either side of the minister's bent, bald head with its gray temples. He went on reading to the end without looking up at the sound of the door opening and footsteps approaching.
"Take this and deliver it," he said to his adjutant, handing over the papers and still not acknowledging the special messenger.

Prince Andrei felt that either Kutuzov's army interested the Minister of War less than the other matters on his desk, or the minister wanted to give that impression. "But it makes absolutely no difference to me," he thought. The minister gathered the remaining papers, straightened them into a neat pile, and finally raised his head. He had a distinctive, intelligent face—but the moment he turned to Prince Andrei, its firm, perceptive expression shifted in a way that was clearly deliberate and habitual. His face assumed the stupid, artificial smile—making no attempt whatsoever to disguise its falseness—of a man who spends his days receiving one petitioner after another.
[Speaking in French] "From Field Marshal Kutuzov?" he asked. "Good news, I hope? An engagement with Mortier? A victory? It was about time!"
He took the dispatch addressed to him and began reading it with a sorrowful expression.
"Oh, my God! My God! Schmidt!" he exclaimed in German. "What a catastrophe! What a catastrophe!"
Having skimmed the dispatch, he laid it on the table and studied Prince Andrei, clearly turning something over in his mind.

"What a tragedy! You say the battle was decisive? But Mortier was not captured." He reflected again. "I'm very glad you've brought good news, though Schmidt's death is a heavy price for this victory. His Majesty will certainly want to see you, but not today. I thank you! You need rest. Come to the levee tomorrow, after the parade. I'll send word, however."
The stupid smile, which had vanished while he was speaking, reappeared on his face.
[Speaking in French] "Goodbye! Thank you very much. His Majesty will most likely wish to see you," he added with a bow.

When Prince Andrei left the palace, he felt that all the excitement and happiness the victory had given him had been surrendered into the indifferent hands of the Minister of War and the polite adjutant. The entire character of his thoughts changed in an instant; the battle now seemed like the memory of some distant event, long past.
